entries.name: Agentic Bug Hunter
entries.use_for: Run AI-assisted recon, vulnerability testing and report writing for bug bounty targets.
entries.why: Covers recon to report, remembers findings across targets, and runs standalone or as a Claude Code plugin.
entries.summary: A toolkit that runs recon, tests for 26 web vulnerability classes, validates findings against a gate, and drafts reports for HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti and Immunefi. Installs from PyPI or as a plugin and uses external tools like nuclei and subfinder.
entries.best_for: Bug bounty hunters who want an agent to drive their usual recon tooling.
entries.not_for: Testing targets you have no permission for. Needs extra CLI tools installed, and the README includes partner sign-up promotions.

entries.name: Android Reverse Engineering Skill
entries.use_for: Decompile Android APK, XAPK, JAR and AAR files and extract the HTTP APIs they use.
entries.why: Recovers Kotlin class names under R8 and handles Retrofit, Ktor, Apollo and Koin.
entries.summary: A Claude Code skill that decompiles Android packages with jadx and Fernflower and pulls out endpoints, auth headers and tokens. It fingerprints the framework first, traces call flows from activities to HTTP, and rebuilds names from Kotlin metadata.
entries.best_for: Documenting or reproducing the API of an app when you lack the source, for apps you are allowed to analyze.
entries.not_for: Windows PowerShell scripts are experimental. Heavily native or non-Android-native apps give less to extract.

entries.name: Anthropic Cybersecurity Skills
entries.use_for: Give coding agents 800+ structured security playbooks mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, NIST and more.
entries.why: Skills use agentskills.io frontmatter with when-to-use, prerequisites and step-by-step verification.
entries.summary: A library of cybersecurity skills for AI agents in the agentskills.io format. Each has YAML frontmatter for discovery, step-by-step Markdown workflows and reference files, covering areas like digital forensics and incident response, mapped to six security frameworks.
entries.best_for: Security teams who want agents following analyst-style workflows with framework references.
entries.not_for: Despite the name, it is a community project and the README does not say Anthropic made it. Review skills before running them against real systems.

entries.name: Anything Analyzer
entries.use_for: Capture web, app and CLI traffic in one place and have an AI analyze the API and crypto flow.
entries.why: Browser capture, a MITM proxy and JS hooks feed one AI analysis session, exposed over MCP.
entries.summary: An Electron app with a built-in browser and a MITM proxy. It records traffic from web pages, desktop apps, scripts and phones into one session. AI then filters and analyzes it for API reverse engineering, security audits or JS crypto. A built-in MCP server lets Claude Desktop or Cursor use it.
entries.best_for: Reverse engineering an API or protocol, or auditing an app, where you want captured traffic explained by an LLM.
entries.not_for: Only use on traffic you are allowed to inspect. Needs an LLM API for analysis. The README is mainly Chinese.

entries.name: Bandit
entries.use_for: Find common security issues in Python code.
entries.why: The standard Python security linter from PyCQA.
entries.summary: Security linter for Python that analyzes code for common security issues. It is the standard PyCQA static analysis tool used in CI and pre-commit.
entries.best_for: Quick static security checks on Python codebases in CI.
entries.not_for: Python only and pattern-based: it produces false positives and does not check dependencies, secrets or runtime behavior.

entries.name: Bumblebee
entries.use_for: Check which developer machines have a package or extension named in a supply-chain advisory.
entries.why: Read-only single Go binary that reads lockfiles and tool metadata without running package managers.
entries.summary: A read-only inventory collector for package, extension and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux endpoints. It reads lockfiles, install metadata, extension manifests and supported MCP configs, and emits NDJSON records. With an exposure catalog it flags exact matches.
entries.best_for: Security teams responding to a named compromised package or extension who need to find affected developer machines fast.
entries.not_for: Not a vulnerability scanner or EDR. It only matches known names and versions, and only on macOS and Linux.

entries.name: Checkov
entries.use_for: Scan Terraform, Kubernetes, Helm, Dockerfiles and more for security misconfigurations
entries.why: Leading open IaC scanner with 1000+ built-in policies and CI integrations
entries.summary: Static analysis tool for infrastructure as code that also does software composition analysis. Scans Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm, Dockerfile, Bicep, ARM, OpenAPI and more with graph-based policies and 1000+ built-in policies.
entries.best_for: Catching cloud misconfigurations and compliance issues in IaC during CI or pre-commit.
entries.not_for: Static scanning only, no runtime visibility; some advanced features are tied to Prisma Cloud, and policy tuning is needed to cut noise.

entries.name: claude-bughunter
entries.use_for: Give Claude Code bug bounty and external red-team methods, payloads and reporting rules.
entries.why: A large skill bundle with per-vulnerability-class hunting skills built from disclosed reports, plus reporting and triage skills.
entries.summary: A bundle of Claude Code skills and slash commands for web bug hunting and external red-team work. Skills load by topic. It covers vulnerability classes, enterprise identity and perimeter attack chains, triage, and evidence hygiene. It installs as a Claude Code plugin or by copying files.
entries.best_for: Security researchers doing authorized bug bounty or external red-team work who want Claude Code to follow a structured methodology.
entries.not_for: Only for authorized testing. It covers the external attack surface and leaves out internal Active Directory attacks.

entries.name: Codex Security
entries.use_for: Scan a repo for security flaws, validate findings and generate fixes from a CLI or TypeScript SDK.
entries.why: Goes from discovery to validated findings and patches, with SARIF export and CI use.
entries.summary: A CLI (cs) and TypeScript SDK that scans repositories, paths or Git changes, validates candidate findings, drafts patches and SECURITY.md policies, imports GitHub alerts, and exports SARIF, JSON or CSV. It can publish to Linear.
entries.best_for: Adding AI-assisted vulnerability finding and fixing to a repo or CI pipeline.
entries.not_for: Offline or login-free use. It requires signing in, Node.js 22.13+ and Python 3.10+.

entries.name: CrowdSec
entries.use_for: Open-source, crowd-powered intrusion prevention that detects and blocks malicious IPs
entries.why: Modern fail2ban successor with shared blocklists and bouncers for Nginx, Traefik, Cloudflare and more
entries.summary: Open-source IDS/IPS, WAF and bot detection that parses logs, detects attacks and shares malicious IPs through a community blocklist. Detection and remediation are decoupled, with bouncers for firewalls, Nginx, Traefik, Cloudflare and others.
entries.best_for: Protecting self-hosted servers and web apps with crowd-sourced IP blocking, as a modern fail2ban replacement.
entries.not_for: Mostly IP-reputation and log-based; not a full application-layer security suite, and sharing signals with the community network is part of the model.

entries.name: ctf-skills
entries.use_for: Give an agent playbooks for solving CTF challenges across web, pwn, crypto, reversing, forensics and OSINT.
entries.why: One skill per category plus a /solve-challenge orchestrator, each listing only the tools it needs.
entries.summary: A set of Agent Skills for capture-the-flag work, covering areas like web exploitation, binary pwn, crypto, reverse engineering, forensics, OSINT and AI/ML attacks. Skills load by context, or you start the orchestrator with /solve-challenge.
entries.best_for: CTF players using Claude Code or other Agent Skills tools who want technique checklists on demand.
entries.not_for: Non-CTF security work or real-world engagements without authorization. Tools you need must be installed separately.

entries.name: CyberStrike
entries.use_for: Running autonomous penetration tests from a terminal using your own LLM provider subscription.
entries.why: Ships 13+ specialized security agents with built-in OWASP methodology instead of being a thin LLM wrapper.
entries.summary: CyberStrike is a terminal-based AI agent for offensive security testing. It installs as an npm package, asks for an LLM provider and API key, then handles reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation and reporting autonomously using agents that follow OWASP WSTG, CIS benchmarks or MASTG/MASVS depending on the target.
entries.best_for: Security teams who want an autonomous, methodology-driven pentest agent that works with any of 150+ LLM providers.
entries.not_for: Not for testing systems you do not own or lack written authorization to test; unauthorized use is illegal.

entries.name: CyberStrikeAI
entries.use_for: Run AI-assisted authorized security testing with agents, 100+ tools, RAG knowledge and attack-chain views.
entries.why: Combines Eino agents, MCP tools, workflows and audit/replay in one Go workspace.
entries.summary: A Go platform for authorized security operations that combines Eino-powered agents, MCP-native tools, RAG knowledge, visual workflows and attack-chain modeling. It ships 100+ tools for scanning, exploitation, forensics and cloud security.
entries.best_for: Security teams that want a governed, auditable AI workspace around their existing pentest tools.
entries.not_for: Only for systems you own or are authorized to test. The README warns to review hardening before enabling high-risk tools such as WebShell or C2.

entries.name: dcg (Destructive Command Guard)
entries.use_for: Block dangerous git and shell commands before AI coding agents run them.
entries.why: Works as a hook for many agents, with 50+ packs and context-aware matching.
entries.summary: dcg is a fast hook that checks commands from AI coding agents and blocks destructive ones such as rm -rf or force pushes. It works with Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor and others. It has packs for databases, Kubernetes, cloud tools and Terraform.
entries.best_for: Protecting a repo or machine from accidental deletion by coding agents, with little setup.
entries.not_for: Not a sandbox. It only inspects commands via agent hooks, and some tools are only partly supported. License is non-standard.

entries.name: DeepAudit
entries.use_for: Audit a code project with cooperating AI agents, check findings in a sandbox and export a report.
entries.why: Uses Orchestrator, Recon, Analysis and Verification agents, and can run on private Ollama models.
entries.summary: A multi-agent code security audit platform with a FastAPI backend and React UI. You import a project; it identifies the stack, analyses risks, verifies findings in a sandbox and exports PDF, Markdown or JSON reports. It aims to cut false positives of classic SAST.
entries.best_for: Teams who want an AI-assisted code audit they can self-host.
entries.not_for: AGPL-3.0 licence. README is Chinese-first. Findings still need human review.

entries.name: deepsec
entries.use_for: Scan large codebases for hard-to-find vulnerabilities with coding agents running in your infrastructure.
entries.why: Fans work out across workers and resumes interrupted runs.
entries.summary: An agent-powered vulnerability scanner you run on your own infrastructure. `npx deepsec init` picks a model, studies the repo, scans and reviews it, keeping state in a `.deepsec/` folder. Large scans fan out to workers and resume where they stopped.
entries.best_for: On-demand security review of big, long-lived repos where deep findings matter more than cost.
entries.not_for: The README warns scans can cost thousands or tens of thousands of dollars on large codebases. Needs a model API key or Vercel AI Gateway.

entries.name: Defending Code Reference Harness
entries.use_for: Learn from or fork a Claude-based pipeline that scans code for defects, triages them and proposes fixes.
entries.why: A reference from Anthropic covering recon, find, triage, report and patch, with skills you can customise.
entries.summary: A reference implementation of an autonomous find-and-fix pipeline for code vulnerabilities with Claude. It includes skills for threat modelling, scanning, triage and patching, plus a scanning harness. It works with any Claude API access, including Bedrock, Vertex or Azure.
entries.best_for: Building your own code-security pipeline and seeing how Anthropic structures one.
entries.not_for: The README says it is not maintained and not accepting contributions. Autonomous triage and patching are open issues. Follow its sandboxing guidance.

entries.name: DOMPurify
entries.use_for: Fast, tolerant XSS sanitizer for HTML, MathML and SVG
entries.why: The trusted HTML sanitizer from security firm Cure53; the default fix for rendering untrusted HTML
entries.summary: DOM-only, fast XSS sanitizer for HTML, MathML and SVG, written in JavaScript. Works in modern browsers and, via a DOM implementation, on the server; maintained by security firm Cure53.
entries.best_for: Safely rendering untrusted or user-supplied HTML in the browser.
entries.not_for: Sanitizes markup only; it is not a general security layer, and Node usage needs jsdom or similar. Legacy browsers are unsupported (it does nothing there).

entries.name: Falco
entries.use_for: Cloud-native runtime threat detection for hosts, containers and Kubernetes
entries.why: CNCF graduated project; eBPF-based detection of suspicious behavior at runtime
entries.summary: Cloud-native runtime security agent for Linux that watches kernel events (syscalls) against custom rules and enriches them with container and Kubernetes metadata, alerting on suspicious behavior. CNCF graduated project.
entries.best_for: Real-time threat detection on hosts, containers and Kubernetes clusters.
entries.not_for: Detection and alerting only, not prevention or blocking; Linux only and needs rule tuning and a downstream SIEM or alert pipeline.

entries.name: Gitleaks
entries.use_for: Detect hardcoded secrets like API keys and passwords in git repos and files.
entries.why: The most popular open-source secret scanner, easy to run in pre-commit and CI.
entries.summary: Tool that detects hardcoded secrets such as API keys and passwords in git repositories and files, easy to run in pre-commit and CI. The README says it is feature complete and receives only security patches, with the author's focus moving to Betterleaks.
entries.best_for: Scanning repos and history for leaked secrets in CI or pre-commit hooks.
entries.not_for: Maintenance mode (no new features per its README); it detects but does not verify whether a secret is live, unlike Kingfisher.

entries.name: Grype
entries.use_for: Vulnerability scanner for container images, filesystems and SBOMs
entries.why: Fast, accurate CVE scanning that pairs with Syft SBOMs; easy to drop into CI
entries.summary: Vulnerability scanner for container images, filesystems and SBOMs. Supports major OS and language ecosystems and Docker, OCI and Singularity formats, and prioritizes findings with EPSS, KEV and risk scoring; pairs with Syft SBOMs.
entries.best_for: Fast CVE scanning in CI for images and dependencies.
entries.not_for: Reports known vulnerabilities only: no secrets, IaC or runtime analysis, and results depend on the vulnerability database.

entries.name: Helmet
entries.use_for: Secure Express/Node apps by setting HTTP security headers like CSP and HSTS
entries.why: Standard one-line hardening middleware for Express, with millions of weekly downloads
entries.summary: Express/Node middleware that sets HTTP security response headers such as Content-Security-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security. app.use(helmet()) sets 13 headers by default.
entries.best_for: One-line baseline header hardening for Express and Connect-style Node apps.
entries.not_for: Headers only: does not replace input validation, auth or CSRF protection. Default CSP may need tuning, and it targets Node middleware stacks.

entries.name: Kingfisher
entries.use_for: Detect secrets in code and history and validate whether they are live.
entries.why: MongoDB-maintained scanner that adds live validation and blast-radius mapping.
entries.summary: Rust secret scanner maintained by MongoDB that detects leaked secrets with hundreds of built-in rules, validates which credentials are live, maps the blast radius of each leak and helps revoke exposed secrets. Apache-2.0.
entries.best_for: Secret scanning that tells you which found credentials are actually active, across code and history.
entries.not_for: Live validation makes outbound calls to providers, which needs care in sensitive environments; newer than gitleaks or trufflehog.

entries.name: Lynis
entries.use_for: Audit Linux, macOS and Unix hosts for security hardening and compliance.
entries.why: Long-standing, agentless host auditing tool with actionable hardening suggestions.
entries.summary: Security auditing tool for Unix-based systems (Linux, macOS, BSD) that runs on the host itself. It performs an in-depth scan of system configuration, installed packages and defenses, then reports findings with hardening suggestions.
entries.best_for: Sysadmins and auditors checking Linux/Unix servers for hardening and compliance gaps (e.g. before audits), without installing agents.
entries.not_for: Not a network or web-app vulnerability scanner and not for Windows hosts. Output is advice to act on manually; it does not auto-remediate. Some features are in the paid Lynis Enterprise.

entries.name: nono
entries.use_for: Run coding agents in a kernel-enforced sandbox with credential and network controls.
entries.why: A single unprivileged binary with audit, rollback and signed skill checks.
entries.summary: An agent runtime security tool. It sandboxes agents and their tools with kernel enforcement, keeps API keys outside the sandbox via proxy injection, filters network access, verifies skills with Sigstore, and records tamper-evident audit logs.
entries.best_for: Running Claude Code, Codex or your own agents on real machines or CI with strict limits.
entries.not_for: Pre-1.0, so APIs may change. Windows is supported only through WSL2.

entries.name: Nuclei
entries.use_for: Scan web apps, APIs and infrastructure for vulnerabilities using YAML templates.
entries.why: Fast template-driven scanner with a huge community template library.
entries.summary: Vulnerability scanner driven by simple YAML templates that describe detection steps for HTTP, DNS, TCP, SSL, WHOIS and other protocols. A large community template library ships with it, and scans run in parallel with request clustering.
entries.best_for: Scanning web apps, APIs and infrastructure for known CVEs and misconfigurations, writing custom checks, and running regression scans in CI/CD.
entries.not_for: Detects what templates cover; it is not a code analyzer or full manual pentest tool. Scanning targets you do not own is illegal, and results depend on template quality.

entries.name: OpenShell
entries.use_for: Run autonomous AI agents in policy-controlled sandboxes with kernel-level limits on files, syscalls and network.
entries.why: Agents never see real credentials, and risky policy changes are formally checked before human review.
entries.summary: OpenShell is a runtime for fleets of autonomous agents. Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox. Kernel controls limit file and system call access, every network connection passes a policy check, and credentials are added only to approved requests. It installs with one script.
entries.best_for: Letting agents install packages, call APIs and use credentials while you control exactly what they can touch.
entries.not_for: Windows without WSL 2 (experimental). It needs Linux, Apple Silicon macOS, and Docker, Podman or virtualization. Version 0.1.x.

entries.name: OSV-Scanner
entries.use_for: Find known vulnerabilities in your project's dependencies using the OSV database.
entries.why: Google's SCA scanner backed by the open, multi-ecosystem OSV.dev database.
entries.summary: CLI frontend to the OSV.dev vulnerability database and OSV-Scalibr. It reads lockfiles, SBOMs and project dependency lists across many languages and package managers and reports known vulnerabilities affecting them.
entries.best_for: Software composition analysis in CI or locally: finding known vulnerable dependencies across multi-language repos using an open database.
entries.not_for: Only finds known, published vulnerabilities in dependencies; it does not analyze your own code for bugs (use a SAST tool) or scan running hosts.

entries.name: OWASP Nettacker
entries.use_for: Automate network and web reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning.
entries.why: OWASP-maintained modular scanning framework; Apache-2.0.
entries.summary: OWASP Python framework for automated network and web reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning. It uses modular scan and brute-force modules, supports multiple targets and outputs, and can run from CLI, API or Docker.
entries.best_for: Automating information gathering, port/service scans and basic vulnerability checks during authorized penetration tests or security assessments.
entries.not_for: Intended only for authorized testing; not a defensive monitoring or code-scanning tool. Coverage and accuracy are narrower than commercial scanners.

entries.name: RAPTOR
entries.use_for: Run an autonomous security research workflow on a codebase or binary using Claude Code.
entries.why: Chains static analysis, LLM vulnerability validation, exploit generation and patch writing in one workflow.
entries.summary: RAPTOR is a security research framework built on Claude Code. It runs Semgrep, optional Coccinelle and CodeQL, deduplicates findings into SARIF, then sends findings through staged LLM validation, exploit generation and patching. Commands like /scan and /agentic run it, with a cost cap per run.
entries.best_for: You do vulnerability research or defensive review and want an agent-driven pipeline you can modify.
entries.not_for: The authors call it not polished software. LLM analysis costs real money. CodeQL has its own license that does not allow commercial use. Powerful offensive tooling, so use only where authorized.

entries.name: RedAmon
entries.use_for: Running an autonomous, human-approved pentest pipeline that triages findings and opens pull requests with fixes.
entries.why: Solves 97.1% of the XBOW web-security benchmark fully black-box, with every solve auditable tool call by tool call.
entries.summary: RedAmon is a self-hosted, Docker-based framework that chains reconnaissance, exploitation and post-exploitation into one pipeline with human approval gates, then triages findings, writes code fixes and opens pull requests. It exposes and consumes MCP servers, so you can plug in extra tools or drive it from Claude Code.
entries.best_for: Teams wanting an autonomous pentest-to-PR pipeline for authorized security testing of their own repositories.
entries.not_for: Never use it to scan or attack systems you do not own or have explicit written permission to test.

entries.name: reverse-skill
entries.use_for: Route an agent's reverse-engineering, pentest or CTF task to the right method and toolchain.
entries.why: Routing rules and regression cases pick between jadx, Frida, IDA and others instead of guessing.
entries.summary: A skill pack for coding agents that sends APK, binary, JS encryption, PCAP and CTF tasks to a matching playbook. It checks available tools, runs a repeatable workflow, and records evidence and findings. It lists 44 routing rules and 175 benchmark cases.
entries.best_for: You use an AI client for authorized security research and want consistent playbooks and tool bootstrapping.
entries.not_for: For authorized testing only. It needs tools such as Java, Node and Python, and the README is dense and partly aimed at AI agents.

entries.name: Sandbox Runtime (srt)
entries.use_for: Run agents, MCP servers or any process with filesystem and network limits, without a container.
entries.why: Uses native OS sandboxing (sandbox-exec, bubblewrap) plus proxy network filtering, secure by default.
entries.summary: A CLI and library that restricts what a process can read, write and reach on the network. It uses sandbox-exec on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux, with proxy-based domain filtering. Config goes in a settings JSON file.
entries.best_for: Sandboxing local MCP servers, coding agents and shell commands quickly, with no container setup.
entries.not_for: Strong isolation needs like untrusted multi-tenant code. It is a beta research preview, so APIs and config may change.

entries.name: security-audit-skill
entries.use_for: Run a multi-phase security audit of a codebase with a coding agent
entries.why: Official Cloudflare skill; findings are independently verified and emitted as machine-readable output.
entries.summary: Coding-agent skill that runs a six-phase security audit: recon, coverage-led hunting with isolated agents, validation by fresh verifiers, structured findings.json output, independent verification and report generation. Seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability harness.
entries.best_for: Single-repo agent-driven vulnerability audits with verified, machine-readable findings.
entries.not_for: Single-repository starting point, not a fleet-scale system. Uses many isolated agents, so token cost and time can be significant; findings still need review.

entries.name: Semgrep
entries.use_for: Scan source code for bugs and security issues with fast, customizable pattern rules.
entries.why: Lightweight, multi-language SAST with a large rule registry; CE is LGPL-2.1.
entries.summary: Static analysis tool that searches code with patterns that look like the source language itself rather than ASTs or regexes. Supports 30+ languages, a large rule registry, and runs in the IDE, pre-commit hooks or CI.
entries.best_for: Fast SAST in CI and pre-commit: custom bug and security rules, enforcing coding standards, and finding insecure patterns across many languages.
entries.not_for: Community Edition analyzes within single files/functions, so it misses cross-file data-flow issues that the paid platform handles. LGPL-2.1 core; some rules have separate licenses.

entries.name: Shannon
entries.use_for: Run an AI pentester that reads your source, attacks a running app and reports proven exploits.
entries.why: Only reports vulnerabilities that have a working proof-of-concept.
entries.summary: Shannon is an autonomous pentester for web apps and APIs. It analyzes source code for attack vectors, then uses browser automation and CLI tools to run real exploits against the running app. The final report includes only vulnerabilities it proved.
entries.best_for: You want on-demand, code-informed pentesting in dev or CI against staging or local apps.
entries.not_for: AGPL-3.0. It changes target state, so use sandboxed data only and never systems you do not own. Findings need human review.

entries.name: SkillSpector
entries.use_for: Scan AI agent skills for vulnerabilities, malicious patterns and risky behavior before installing.
entries.why: NVIDIA-maintained scanner for the agent-skill supply chain; Apache-2.0.
entries.summary: Security scanner for AI agent skills (as used by Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI). It analyzes skill packages for vulnerabilities, malicious patterns and risky behavior before they are installed, as part of NVIDIA's verified-skills pipeline.
entries.best_for: Vetting third-party agent skills before installing them, or adding a pre-install safety check to an agent skill supply chain.
entries.not_for: Scoped to agent skills only; it is not a general code, dependency or container scanner. Heuristic detection cannot guarantee a skill is safe.

entries.name: Syft
entries.use_for: Generate SBOMs (SPDX, CycloneDX) from container images and filesystems
entries.why: The most used open SBOM generator; the foundation for supply-chain scanning pipelines
entries.summary: CLI tool and Go library that generates a Software Bill of Materials from container images, filesystems and archives. Supports many packaging ecosystems and image formats, and outputs CycloneDX, SPDX or Syft JSON.
entries.best_for: Producing SBOMs for images and repos in CI, and as the input to a vulnerability scanner such as Grype.
entries.not_for: Only inventories packages; it does not find vulnerabilities by itself (pair with Grype or Trivy). Not a runtime monitoring tool.

entries.name: T3MP3ST
entries.use_for: Run a multi-agent offensive security workflow, from recon to exploit to report, with your own coding agent.
entries.why: Reuses the agent you already run, or local models, and publishes benchmark results it says you can recompute.
entries.summary: A multi-agent offensive-security framework with a browser War Room and a CLI. It drives Claude Code, Codex or local models against authorized targets across web apps, CTFs, source code and OSS vulnerability hunting.
entries.best_for: Authorized security testing and research where you want an agent swarm doing recon and exploitation.
entries.not_for: Unauthorized targets or production systems. AGPL-3.0, and some areas such as smart contracts are reproduction, not novel discovery.

entries.name: Trivy
entries.use_for: Scan containers, filesystems, repos, IaC and Kubernetes for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.
entries.why: All-in-one, widely adopted scanner that drops easily into CI; Apache-2.0.
entries.summary: Versatile scanner that targets container images, filesystems, remote git repos, VM images and Kubernetes. It finds vulnerable OS and language packages, IaC misconfigurations, secrets and license issues, and can generate SBOMs.
entries.best_for: One tool in CI for container, IaC and dependency scanning across Docker, Kubernetes and repos.
entries.not_for: Detection depth per area is shallower than specialized tools (dedicated SAST, secrets verification, DAST). It is not a runtime protection or web-app pentest tool.

entries.name: TruffleHog
entries.use_for: Find, verify and analyze leaked credentials in git, CI, cloud storage and more
entries.why: Verifies detected secrets against live APIs to cut false positives; 800+ detectors
entries.summary: Secrets scanner that finds leaked credentials in git history, CI, cloud storage, chat and other sources. It has 800+ detectors and verifies findings against live APIs to reduce false positives, plus can analyze key permissions.
entries.best_for: Auditing repos and org data for leaked API keys and passwords, pre-commit/CI secret scanning, and incident response on suspected leaks.
entries.not_for: Only looks for secrets, not code or dependency vulnerabilities. Verification makes live calls to third-party APIs, which may be unwanted. Enterprise features are separate.

entries.name: TrustTunnel
entries.use_for: Self-host a VPN endpoint whose traffic looks like normal HTTPS, with ready-made clients.
entries.why: Born in AdGuard VPN, it tunnels TCP, UDP and ICMP over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or QUIC.
entries.summary: An open-source VPN protocol and server, with a client library, CLI and GUI apps in sister repos. It mimics ordinary web traffic to resist throttling and deep-packet inspection. The server runs on Linux and macOS and can serve per-user config over HTTPS.
entries.best_for: Running your own VPN server, or embedding the client library, where plain VPN traffic gets blocked.
entries.not_for: A turnkey consumer VPN service. You host and manage the server yourself, and clients are separate repositories.

entries.name: User Scanner
entries.use_for: Check where an email or username is registered across thousands of sites for OSINT work.
entries.why: Covers 2700+ scan vectors with reports in JSON, CSV and PDF, and has a built-in MCP server.
entries.summary: A Python OSINT tool that checks emails on 210+ sites and usernames on 2500+ platforms, scrapes profile metadata, generates alias permutations, and pivots on found handles. Uses httpx and curl_cffi, and can run as an MCP server.
entries.best_for: Security research, investigations and checking your own digital footprint.
entries.not_for: Anything involving people who have not agreed to be searched. Site checks break when sites change, and some scans use TLS fingerprint impersonation.

entries.name: vphone-cli
entries.use_for: Run a virtual iPhone on an Apple Silicon Mac for security research and debugging.
entries.why: Uses Apple's Virtualization.framework with a GUI, cloning, backups and a local automation API.
entries.summary: vphone-cli runs iOS in a virtual machine using Apple's Virtualization.framework and PCC research VMs. It gives a graphical window, patched firmware, VM export, import and cloning, and an optional local HTTP and WebSocket automation API. It needs no Xcode, Python or Homebrew at runtime.
entries.best_for: iOS security researchers and reverse engineers who want a local virtual device.
entries.not_for: General app testing. It needs a physical Apple Silicon Mac on macOS 15+, relaxed debugging security settings, and about 64 GB disk per VM.

entries.name: VulnClaw
entries.use_for: Run an AI agent that does penetration testing from a natural-language request and writes a report.
entries.why: A model-led agent loop with MCP tools and a gate that rejects invented flags.
entries.summary: A Python CLI agent that goes from recon to vuln discovery, exploitation and report generation. It stores tool output as evidence, checks claimed findings against real output, and works with 13 LLM providers and MCP tool servers.
entries.best_for: Authorized pentests, CTFs, security teaching and red-team exercises.
entries.not_for: Only for systems you are allowed to test. Needs an LLM API. Automated exploitation can be unsafe on production targets.

entries.name: Vuls
entries.use_for: Scan Linux/FreeBSD servers, containers and libraries for known CVEs without agents.
entries.why: Agentless vulnerability scanner for server fleets with multiple data sources.
entries.summary: Agentless vulnerability scanner for Linux and FreeBSD written in Go. It checks servers, containers and libraries against multiple vulnerability data sources and reports known CVEs over SSH without installing software on targets.
entries.best_for: Teams managing fleets of Linux/FreeBSD servers who want agentless CVE reporting and notifications.
entries.not_for: Report-only: it does not update vulnerable packages. Not for Windows or web-app testing, and requires setting up vulnerability databases.

entries.name: ZAP
entries.use_for: Test web applications for vulnerabilities with an intercepting proxy and automated scans.
entries.why: The most widely used free DAST tool, scriptable and CI-friendly.
entries.summary: ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy) by Checkmarx is a free, open source web app security scanner. It automatically finds security vulnerabilities in web applications during development and testing, and also supports manual testing by pentesters. Apache 2.0 licensed.
entries.best_for: Scanning your own web applications for vulnerabilities during development or CI, and manual penetration testing.
entries.not_for: Static code analysis or dependency scanning; it tests running web apps. Only scan applications you are authorized to test.
